title: Extract MOSFET output resistance from a DC sweep
summary: Extract the local slope of drain current and turn it into small-signal output resistance.

quiz.instructions: Why should you use a narrow drain-voltage interval in saturation?
options: A local slope describes small-signal resistance at this bias
A sweep endpoint always equals threshold
Output resistance is the DC ratio VDS/ID
quiz.explanation: The inverse slope ΔVDS/ΔID describes the incremental resistance. VDS/ID is a different quantity.

tasks.title: Measure the starter
tasks.instructions: Run the starter with its original values and open Results. Extract the local slope of drain current and turn it into small-signal output resistance.

tasks.title: Verify the comparison
tasks.instructions: Tune VGATE and extract 300–500 kΩ using the measured slope from 0.8 to 1.2 V. Keep the current at 0.8 V between 15 and 100 µA.

reflection: Compare your hand estimate with the captured measurements. Explain the difference or the model assumption that matters most.

teaching.concept: The inverse slope ΔVDS/ΔID describes the incremental resistance. VDS/ID is a different quantity.
teaching.worked_example: A 400 mV change that moves drain current by 1 µA gives 400 kΩ.
teaching.try_next: Compare the low-VDS triode slope with the .8–1.2 V interval.
teaching.interview: At fixed VGS, what makes the saturation trace slope upward?
teaching.artifact: Save both sweep points and report the bias and extracted resistance.

title: Make body effect visible
summary: Sweep gate bias with the body tied to the source and with a reverse-biased body.

quiz.instructions: How does increased reverse body bias shift the NMOS gate voltage required for the same drain current?
options: It raises the required gate voltage
It lowers the required gate voltage
It makes gate voltage irrelevant
quiz.explanation: Increasing VSB increases the effective NMOS threshold in this teaching model.

tasks.title: Measure the starter
tasks.instructions: Run the starter with its original values and open Results. Sweep gate bias with the body tied to the source and with a reverse-biased body.

tasks.title: Verify the comparison
tasks.instructions: Set VSB to produce a 130–230 mV positive shift in gate voltage at the 10 µA criterion.

reflection: Compare your hand estimate with the captured measurements. Explain the difference or the model assumption that matters most.

teaching.concept: Increasing VSB increases the effective NMOS threshold in this teaching model.
teaching.worked_example: A 10 µA constant-current criterion compares both curves without relying on the first visible current.
teaching.try_next: Try a smaller reverse bias and plot the extracted shift against VSB.
teaching.interview: Why does tying body to source at the symbol change the measured threshold?
teaching.artifact: Save both current sweeps and record the gate voltage at 10 µA.

title: Compare MOSFET and resistor loads
summary: Match the output DC bias of two common-source stages and compare their small-signal gain.

quiz.instructions: At the same bias, which load typically has a lower incremental resistance here?
options: The diode-connected PMOS
The open input terminal
The resistor in every circuit
quiz.explanation: The diode-connected PMOS presents an incremental resistance near 1/gm, in parallel with its output resistance.

tasks.title: Measure the starter
tasks.instructions: Run the starter with its original values and open Results. Match the output DC bias of two common-source stages and compare their small-signal gain.

tasks.title: Verify the comparison
tasks.instructions: Adjust RLOAD to bring the output biases within 120 mV. Show that the resistive stage has more than twice the gain at 100 Hz.

reflection: Compare your hand estimate with the captured measurements. Explain the difference or the model assumption that matters most.

teaching.concept: The diode-connected PMOS presents an incremental resistance near 1/gm, in parallel with its output resistance.
teaching.worked_example: At 60 µA, a 0.9 V drop suggests a resistor of about 15 kΩ.
teaching.try_next: Try a different input bias and repeat the DC matching before comparing gain.
teaching.interview: Why does a diode-connected transistor behave differently from an ideal current-source load?
teaching.artifact: Keep the matched DC voltages and AC gain comparison.

title: Measure a complementary transmission gate
summary: Measure switch resistance over signal common mode with a 5 mV test drop.

quiz.instructions: Which transistor helps an NMOS switch pass a high signal level?
options: A parallel PMOS driven by the complementary control
A series NMOS with the same drive
A diode connected across the gate
quiz.explanation: The PMOS can conduct strongly at high common-mode voltage as the NMOS loses overdrive.

tasks.title: Measure the starter
tasks.instructions: Run the starter with its original values and open Results. Measure switch resistance over signal common mode with a 5 mV test drop.

tasks.title: Verify the comparison
tasks.instructions: Size MP to keep transmission-gate resistance below 1.9 kΩ at the three test voltages with a max/min ratio at most 2.6.

reflection: Compare your hand estimate with the captured measurements. Explain the difference or the model assumption that matters most.

teaching.concept: The PMOS can conduct strongly at high common-mode voltage as the NMOS loses overdrive.
teaching.worked_example: Measure test-source current at a 5 mV drop and calculate resistance as 5 mV divided by current.
teaching.try_next: Try a different PMOS width and compare resistance near mid-rail and the high end.
teaching.interview: Why does a wider PMOS help one part of the curve and change the middle as well?
teaching.artifact: Save NMOS-only and transmission-gate resistance at 0.2, 0.9, and 1.6 V.

title: Compare thermal and flicker noise
summary: Run matched MOS noise benches with flicker disabled and enabled. Compare amplitude spectral density and infer the flicker contribution.

quiz.instructions: How do independent thermal and flicker contributions add?
options: Their power spectral densities add
Their amplitude densities always add directly
Their corner frequencies add
quiz.explanation: Subtract the squared thermal density from the squared total density, then take the square root.

tasks.title: Verify the comparison
tasks.instructions: Measure the thermal and total spectra. Verify that inferred flicker density dominates at 100 Hz and falls below thermal at 1 MHz.

reflection: Compare your hand estimate with the captured measurements. Explain the difference or the model assumption that matters most.

teaching.concept: Subtract the squared thermal density from the squared total density, then take the square root.
teaching.worked_example: A 5 nV/√Hz total with a 3 nV/√Hz thermal floor implies 4 nV/√Hz of independent flicker noise.
teaching.try_next: Sketch what happens to the crossing when the flicker coefficient changes by a factor of four.
teaching.interview: How does selecting a lower measurement band change which noise source dominates?
teaching.artifact: Save the paired output noise spectra and the inferred flicker readings.

title: Explore leakage in a bias network
summary: A reverse-biased diode leaks into a high-impedance bias node. Compare room and hot operating points.

quiz.instructions: For fixed leakage current, what reduces the bias error?
options: Lowering the bias resistance
Raising the bias resistance
Changing the voltage probe label
quiz.explanation: The same leakage current causes a smaller DC error through a lower resistance.

tasks.title: Measure the starter
tasks.instructions: Run the starter with its original values and open Results. A reverse-biased diode leaks into a high-impedance bias node. Compare room and hot operating points.

tasks.title: Verify the comparison
tasks.instructions: Keep the 85 °C bias within 50 mV of 1.2 V and verify the leakage rises by more than 10× relative to room temperature.

reflection: Compare your hand estimate with the captured measurements. Explain the difference or the model assumption that matters most.

teaching.concept: The same leakage current causes a smaller DC error through a lower resistance.
teaching.worked_example: A leakage current of 100 nA through 100 kΩ causes about 10 mV of error.
teaching.try_next: Compare 27 °C and 85 °C at both bias resistances and discuss loading of the reference.
teaching.interview: Why can a circuit work at room temperature even if its bias network is weak?
teaching.artifact: Save room and hot voltage and infer leakage from the resistor drop.

title: Design a common-mode feedback loop
summary: Sense the output average and correct it without disturbing the differential signal in a fully differential behavioral circuit.

quiz.instructions: Which signal should the common-mode loop correct?
options: The average of the two output voltages
The difference between the output voltages
The input sine-wave frequency
quiz.explanation: Both outputs move together under a common-mode correction, so their difference is preserved in a symmetric plant.

tasks.title: Measure the starter
tasks.instructions: Run the starter with its original values and open Results. Sense the output average and correct it without disturbing the differential signal in a fully differential behavioral circuit.

tasks.title: Verify the comparison
tasks.instructions: Tune gain and compensation. Limit common-mode error to 10 mV at 18 µs, recover to within 2 mV of the final level in 2 µs, and keep differential output at 200 mV ± 1 mV.

reflection: Compare your hand estimate with the captured measurements. Explain the difference or the model assumption that matters most.

teaching.concept: Both outputs move together under a common-mode correction, so their difference is preserved in a symmetric plant.
teaching.worked_example: With DC loop gain 19, a 120 mV common-mode disturbance leaves about 6 mV of error.
teaching.try_next: Try a smaller loop gain and record the change in correction and recovery.
teaching.interview: How would asymmetry cause the common-mode correction to affect differential output?
teaching.artifact: Save open-loop and closed-loop transients and report the output difference.

title: Separate charge injection and clock feedthrough
summary: Measure the two sources of held-voltage error separately and then with both present.

quiz.instructions: Which term remains when the injected charge packet is disabled?
options: Capacitive feedthrough from the clock
Channel charge injection
Both terms disappear in a real switch
quiz.explanation: Clock feedthrough comes from capacitive coupling. The separate packet models channel charge delivered to the held node.

tasks.title: Measure the starter
tasks.instructions: Run the starter with its original values and open Results. Measure the two sources of held-voltage error separately and then with both present.

tasks.title: Verify the comparison
tasks.instructions: Size CHOLD so the combined held step is at most 35 mV. Keep both isolated errors visible and close the sum within 10 mV.

reflection: Compare your hand estimate with the captured measurements. Explain the difference or the model assumption that matters most.

teaching.concept: Clock feedthrough comes from capacitive coupling. The separate packet models channel charge delivered to the held node.
teaching.worked_example: A 20 fC packet deposited on 1 pF changes its voltage by 20 mV.
teaching.try_next: Increase the hold capacitance again and predict the penalty for reacquisition time in a real sampling circuit.
teaching.interview: What controlled comparisons let you separate these two effects in a model?
teaching.artifact: Keep the isolated and combined transient cases and compare the three held-voltage steps.
